actors.name: Nikita Khrushchev (First Secretary of CPSU / Premier of USSR)
actors.stance: Covertly offensive deterrence strategy (intimidate US to protect Cuba without provoking outright war):contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
actors.ideology: Marxism-Leninism (de-Stalinized reformist); advocates 'peaceful coexistence' with the West:contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1} but willing to risk bold moves to support world socialism:contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}:contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}
actors.risk_tolerance: High (willing to take significant risks like secret missile deployment, though hoping to avoid nuclear war):contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}:contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}
actors.conflict_avoidance: Medium (does not want direct war:contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}, but prepared to engage in brinkmanship rather than capitulation)
actors.diplomacy_preference: Backchannel and personal diplomacy (secret moves, private letters) over open public negotiations; initial denial/deception followed by negotiation when confronted
actors.military_preference: Strategic deterrence (use nuclear placement to deter enemy, avoid first use of strategic nukes:contentReference[oaicite:7]{index=7}; if conflict erupts, consider limited tactical force rather than all-out strike):contentReference[oaicite:8]{index=8}
goals: Deter U.S. invasion of Cuba and safeguard the Castro regime:contentReference[oaicite:9]{index=9}:contentReference[oaicite:10]{index=10}
Redress strategic imbalance with the U.S. by forward-deploying nuclear missiles (gain leverage and prestige):contentReference[oaicite:11]{index=11}:contentReference[oaicite:12]{index=12}
Maintain Soviet credibility as leader of the socialist camp by standing firm in the Western Hemisphere:contentReference[oaicite:13]{index=13}
constraints: Incomplete deployment of missiles in Cuba as of Oct 21 (many missiles not yet operational):contentReference[oaicite:14]{index=14}
Need to avoid triggering a U.S.–Soviet nuclear war (fear that retaliation could escalate uncontrollably):contentReference[oaicite:15]{index=15}
Reliance on secrecy and surprise – early exposure of the plan limits Soviet bargaining position:contentReference[oaicite:16]{index=16}

behavior_algorithm.decision_rule: Primarily top-down: Khrushchev makes key decisions after consulting the Presidium (one-man dominant leadership with some collective input):contentReference[oaicite:17]{index=17}:contentReference[oaicite:18]{index=18}
behavior_algorithm.utility_formula: Maximize Soviet strategic advantage and revolutionary credibility minus probability of catastrophic war (U = security gain + ideological prestige – escalation risk)

trigger_thresholds.US_naval_blockade: Elevate military alert status; call urgent leadership deliberation (crisis mode):contentReference[oaicite:19]{index=19}:contentReference[oaicite:20]{index=20}
trigger_thresholds.US_invasion_Cuba: Initiate military response, including possible tactical nuclear use on invading forces (last-resort retaliation)
trigger_thresholds.diplomatic_resolution_offer: If a viable compromise is offered guaranteeing Cuba’s security, shift to negotiation to avert war

actors.name: Communist Party of the Soviet Union (Party Presidium)
actors.stance: Assertive defensive posture (endorses missile deployment to protect Cuba and challenge U.S. influence, but prefers to avoid direct great-power war)
actors.ideology: Marxism-Leninism (collective leadership) – generally supportive of Khrushchev’s line of aiding world socialism while pursuing 'peaceful coexistence' with caution
actors.risk_tolerance: Medium (willing to approve a risky Cuba gambit, but members have mixed concern about provoking the U.S.):contentReference[oaicite:21]{index=21}
actors.conflict_avoidance: Medium-High (collectively keen to avoid full-scale war that could devastate the USSR, yet unwilling to abandon Cuba or appear weak in the face of U.S. pressure)
actors.diplomacy_preference: Official denial and propaganda in public; private willingness to negotiate a resolution if core socialist gains can be preserved (e.g. secret talks via Khrushchev):contentReference[oaicite:22]{index=22}
actors.military_preference: Strategic deterrence and defensive readiness; endorse show of force (missile presence) but favor reactive use of force only if attacked (no deliberate first strike)
goals: Ensure Cuba remains a socialist ally and symbol of Soviet commitment (prevent a U.S.-backed regime change):contentReference[oaicite:23]{index=23}
Maintain Soviet prestige and credibility in the Cold War and among communist allies by standing up to U.S. threats:contentReference[oaicite:24]{index=24}
Avoid nuclear conflict while securing a favorable outcome (seek a face-saving resolution that protects Soviet interests)
constraints: Requirement for collective agreement among Presidium members (internal consensus needed, which can slow or moderate decisions)
Ideological obligation to support allies and not appear to capitulate to capitalism, balanced against the existential threat of nuclear war
Limited strategic reach relative to the U.S. (acknowledgment of American nuclear superiority necessitates caution):contentReference[oaicite:25]{index=25}

behavior_algorithm.decision_rule: Collective deliberation (Presidium consensus-building) with deference to the First Secretary’s leadership in final decisions:contentReference[oaicite:26]{index=26}
behavior_algorithm.utility_formula: Balance revolutionary duty and state security against war risk (Utility = ideological success + strategic security – probability of war)

trigger_thresholds.US_military_action: If U.S. attacks Cuba or Soviet forces, consensus to escalate military response (shift to war footing)
trigger_thresholds.imminent_nuclear_war: If nuclear war appears unavoidable, prioritize de-escalation or diplomatic outreach to prevent mutual destruction
trigger_thresholds.negotiable_settlement: If a compromise is possible that ensures Cuba’s security and saves face, support a diplomatic solution over continued conflict

actors.name: Soviet Armed Forces (High Command)
actors.stance: Hawkish, deterrence-oriented (supports aggressive nuclear deployment in Cuba to strengthen Soviet strategic position; prepared to respond with force if provoked):contentReference[oaicite:27]{index=27}
actors.ideology: Loyal Marxist-Leninist, focused on defense of the socialist state; tends toward hardline security views (emphasizing military strength over political nuance):contentReference[oaicite:28]{index=28}
actors.risk_tolerance: Medium (initially confident the U.S. would not risk major confrontation:contentReference[oaicite:29]{index=29}, but cognizant of the catastrophic risks of nuclear war)
actors.conflict_avoidance: Low–Medium (the military is prepared to fight if ordered, less inclined to back down, though aware of modern war’s destructive capacity):contentReference[oaicite:30]{index=30}
actors.diplomacy_preference: Prefers displays of strength and resolve over diplomacy; leaves negotiations to political leaders while signaling readiness (e.g. continuing deployments, high alert drills)
actors.military_preference: Emphasis on strategic deterrence rather than preemptive strike:contentReference[oaicite:31]{index=31}; maintain robust defense and readiness to use tactical nuclear weapons if war breaks out, but view nuclear arms primarily as a deterrent of war
goals: Establish a stronger strategic foothold in the Western Hemisphere to deter U.S. aggression (successfully deploy and secure nuclear missiles in Cuba):contentReference[oaicite:32]{index=32}
Protect the Soviet homeland and allies by offsetting U.S. nuclear superiority (improve the nuclear balance via forward deployment):contentReference[oaicite:33]{index=33}
Fulfill Operation Anadyr (the Cuba deployment) successfully to demonstrate Soviet military capability and resolve
constraints: Inferior strategic nuclear arsenal compared to the U.S., limiting first-strike options and necessitating caution:contentReference[oaicite:34]{index=34}
Strict civilian control – must await political directives (cannot act independently to initiate hostilities):contentReference[oaicite:35]{index=35}
Logistical challenges of overseas deployment (distance, covert transport, tropical climate impacts on equipment, etc.):contentReference[oaicite:36]{index=36}

behavior_algorithm.decision_rule: Hierarchical command structure: execute orders from top political leadership; internal decisions driven by military protocol and threat assessments
behavior_algorithm.utility_formula: Prioritize mission success and force preservation minus risk of overwhelming retaliation (U = mission success probability + deterrence value – likelihood of devastating counterstrike)

trigger_thresholds.high_alert_order: If political leadership orders combat alert (due to U.S. escalation), move to full readiness and prepare nuclear assets for possible use
trigger_thresholds.direct_attack: If Soviet forces or Cuban ally are attacked, retaliate per war plans (including tactical nuclear response if authorized)
trigger_thresholds.political_deescalation: If leadership seeks a deal or stand-down, comply with withdrawal/stand-down directives even if militarily disadvantageous
